newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egyptian cotton back on world market in force.
newsitem.headline: Egyptian cotton back on world market in force.

text.p: Egyptian cotton exporters hope a bumper harvest and a volte face in the government's trade policy will lure back international buyers and revive Egypt's domination of the world market for quality fibre.

Farmers are just beginning to pick this year's crop, estimated at 350,000 tonnes compared with 260,000 tonnes last year. With stocks of 40,000 tonnes left over from last year Egypt may have bumper supplies of 400,000 tonnes.

The government's decision to let farmers export all types of cotton, including those traditionally reserved for domestic use, is expected to increase by eight-fold the amount slated for export this year to 150,000 tonnes from last year's 19,000.
Exports will also be helped by the government's recent decision to let spinning companies import cotton from anywhere in the world provided it meets disease and control regulations.

The state took the export liberalisation decision in February, ending years of diverting the valuable long-staple kinds for use in the textile industry. Now the industry can import cheaper varieties instead.
"The (export) amount this year is tremendous," said Saeed Mahmoud Haggag, chairman of the Alexandria Cotton Exporters Association (Alcotexa), which sets export prices.

"We're entering the market this year with all we've got and hope the government will not change its mind about this policy. International buyers need continuity and we need that to regain our former glory," Haggag told Reuters.
The government has set a minimum price of 500 pounds ($147) for 50 kg, the equivalent of 133 centilibres (U.S. cents a lb), to encourage Egyptian farmers to grow it.
Now private sector traders are complaining that this minimum is keeping them out of the market.

"It's not really fair but we're hoping to sell a lot to make up the difference and this year our prices are good and we think competitive," said a private cotton exporter, who asked not to be named. State buyers dominate the revived Mina al-Basal cotton exchange in Alexandria, where farmers go to sell their crop.
Egypt's plentiful supply is bound to drive international prices down, which would also allow it to dominate international markets, private importers said.
With the minimum state price in place, the government may have to compensate traders from its own pocket through a government-run fund.

Alcotexa, which groups 11 state-owned cotton exporters and seven private ones, announced this week's export prices for nine varieties between 224 and 100 centilibres (U.S. cents per lb). Last year prices ranged between 237 and 183 centilibres.

"We can't read runes or palms but we're hoping to sell a modest 75,000 tonnes. Our main competition is America and they have the advantage of adjusting prices instantly on demand. We have to do it by consensus," Haggag said.
Agriculture and trade ministry officials have said they are looking into samples of Syrian, Russian and Turkish cotton, thoroughly investigating them for pests and diseases before allowing imports.
